column11: There is a lack of coherence throughout the text that makes it extremely difficult to follow -- e.g., how many people are there in the village? There is no one in the village, but no, that is false, there are two women named Sara, but no, one of them had died in August. The fragment is rambling and -- I realise that this sounds strange, as it is a generated text -- tries to make an impression of being sophisticated.
column19: This story has the merit of actually going somewhere. I feel that with the right edits -- mostly concerning banal or incoherent comparisons and metaphors -- this might be the start of something; with A LOT of edits, it might even be good. I found at least one fragment genuinely funny (the one with the person coming back from the dead), and the general premise of someone working in a department for misplaced documents, handling administrative mistakes, is good.
column27: This story does not seem to me to include so many easily-identifiable traits of AI writing -- I think that if I received this without any additional information, I'd say it was by a slightly pretentious but overall gifted late high-schooler (or early undergrad). I cannot put my finger on the exact reason why, but I had the feeling that when the descriptions start referring to details of activities (e.g., playing the piano), they read like written by someone who never did or properly observed those things.
column35: At this point of the experiment everything reads like AI, but there is a typically ChatGPT-eseque first sentence ("not as,... but as") that made this problematic from the outset. It is interesting to ask GenAI to do synaesthesia, and I feel that it fails horribly. This story combines the pretentious nonsense of A with the lack of practical experience (or perhaps the lack of ability to write about practical experience) of C.
column36: I think story B surprised me most, because I found it somewhat original and interesting -- there were points where I really wanted to know about the characters. Also, as a translator I worked with some really pretentious and unrefined literature [genre detail redacted for respondent privacy], and some of these stories (especially A and D) read, in parts, as if they were written by some version of these authors.
